blocks.text: On entering he nearly fell, for behind the door there was yet another step. "They don't show much consideration for the public," he said. "They show no consideration whatsoever," said the court usher, "just look at the waiting room here." It was a long corridor from which roughly carpentered doors led to the separate departments of the attic. Although there was no direct access of light, it was nevertheless not completely dark, for several departments had, facing the corridor, instead of solid plank walls, mere wooden latticework reaching, it is true, up to the ceiling, through which some light penetrated and through which one could also see individual officials writing at tables or standing right against the latticework and observing the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were, probably because it was Sunday, only a few people in the corridor. They made a very modest impression. At almost regular intervals from one another they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches that were set along both sides of the corridor. All were negligently dressed, although most of them, judging by their facial expression, bearing, style of beard, and many small, scarcely ascertainable details, belonged to the upper classes. As there were no coat hooks provided, they had placed their hats, probably one following the example of the other, under the bench. When those who sat nearest the door caught sight of K. and the court usher, they rose in greeting; as those next in line saw this, they believed they must greet them too, so that everyone rose as the two walked past. They never stood completely upright, their backs were bowed, their knees bent, they stood like street beggars. K. waited for the court usher, who was walking a little behind him, and said: "How humiliated they must be." "Yes," said the court usher, "they are accused men, all those you see here are accused men." "Really!" said K. "Then they are my colleagues, after all." And he turned to the nearest one, a tall, slender, already almost gray-haired man. "What are you waiting for here?" K. asked politely. The unexpected address, however, threw the man into confusion, which looked all the more embarrassing as he was evidently a man of the world who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not easily relinquish the superiority he had acquired over many others. Here, however, he did not know how to answer so simple a question and looked over at the others as if they were obliged to help him, and as if no one could demand an answer from him if this help were not forthcoming. At that the court usher stepped up and said, in order to calm and encourage the man: "The gentleman here is only asking what you are waiting for. Do answer." The court usher's voice, which was probably familiar to him, had a better effect: "I am waiting—" he began and faltered. Evidently he had chosen this opening in order to answer the exact phrasing of the question, but could not now find how to continue. Some of those waiting had drawn nearer and stood around the group; the court usher said to them: "Away, away, clear the corridor." They drew back a little, though not all the way to their former seats. Meanwhile the man who had been questioned had collected himself and even answered with a slight smile: "A month ago I submitted several motions for evidence in my case and am waiting for them to be dealt with." "You seem to be taking a great deal of trouble," said K. "Yes," said the man, "it is my case, after all." "Not everyone thinks as you do," said K., "I, for example, am also accused, yet, as I hope to be saved, I have neither filed a motion for evidence nor undertaken anything else of the sort. Do you really consider that necessary?" "I do not know for certain," said the man, once more in complete uncertainty; he evidently believed K. was making a joke at his expense, and therefore, out of fear of committing some new blunder, he would probably have preferred to repeat his former answer in full, yet under K.'s impatient gaze he said only, "as for myself, I have filed motions for evidence." "You don't believe, I suppose, that I am accused," K. asked. "Oh, please, certainly," said the man, stepping a little to one side, yet in his answer there was not belief, only fear. "So you don't believe me?" asked K., and, unconsciously prompted to it by the man's humble demeanor, seized him by the arm as though he wished to force him to believe. He did not mean to cause him pain and had indeed taken hold of him only very lightly, yet the man cried out as if K. had grasped him not with two fingers, but with red-hot tongs. This ridiculous screaming finally exhausted K.'s patience; if the man did not believe he was accused, so much the better; perhaps he even took him for a judge. And now, in parting, he really did grasp him more firmly, pushed him back onto the bench, and walked on. "Most of the accused are that sensitive," said the court usher. Behind them, almost all those waiting now gathered around the man, who had already stopped screaming, and seemed to be questioning him closely about the incident. Coming toward K. now was a warder, recognizable chiefly by a saber whose scabbard, at least to judge by its color, was made of aluminum. K. marveled at it and even reached out his hand to it. The warder, who had come because of the screaming, asked what had happened. The court usher sought to reassure him with a few words, but the warder declared that he must nevertheless go and see for himself, saluted, and walked on with very hurried yet very short steps, measured out, probably, by gout.
